passage: Tuan, fifteen, did his maths homework by an oil lamp again because the village power cut had lasted three nights. In the Mekong delta his family grew rice, and his father wanted him to help with the harvest. Tuan wanted to be an engineer in Ho Chi Minh City. A volunteer from Spain, Pablo, taught English on Saturdays at the village hall. When Tuan asked how to get into a good university, Pablo did not promise anything. He said, "Coaching is expensive. But the hall has past papers and a computer. Let's plan how you use them, step by step." Tuan copied the plan into a small notebook. That night under the lamp he solved the first past-paper question and whispered, "One down." His father, passing, saw the light and quietly set down a glass of water.

qa.q: What did Pablo say the village hall has?
qa.a: Pablo said the hall has past papers and a computer.

qa.q: What is Tuan feeling as he whispers "One down"?
qa.a: Tuan feels determined and quietly hopeful, working by an oil lamp despite the power cut.

qa.q: Which choice by Pablo helped Tuan?
qa.a: Pablo did not promise anything. He offered a step-by-step plan using the past papers and computer at the hall.

qa.q: How might Tuan's father feel as he sets down the glass of water?
qa.a: Probably caring and quietly supportive, even though he wanted Tuan to help with the harvest.

grounding: A rural teenager studies by lamp and dreams of a city engineering career, slowed by money and family need, and helped by a local mentor.

passage: In the village library room of the community centre, Nazia, fifteen, sat with her notebook open long after the others had gone. She wanted to be a district collector and had no money for city coaching. Farida, the retired teacher who ran the library on weekday evenings, saw her there again. "Same chapter?" she asked. "Yes, ma'am. I keep reading, but I don't know if I'm doing it right." Farida pulled out an old study guide and a newspaper. "We can't buy coaching, but we can build a routine. One hour of current affairs, one hour of maths, and every Sunday I'll check your answers." Nazia frowned. "My mother needs me at home after dinner." "Then we start at four, before you go home." Nazia nodded slowly and wrote "4 pm" at the top of the page.

qa.q: At what time does Farida suggest they start?
qa.a: Farida suggests they start at four, before Nazia goes home.

qa.q: What is Nazia feeling as she says she doesn't know if she is doing it right?
qa.a: Nazia is determined but unsure and a little worried, since she has no coaching to check her work.

qa.q: Which choice by Farida helped Nazia keep going?
qa.a: Farida built a routine from an old study guide and a newspaper, offered to check answers every Sunday and moved the start to four to fit Nazia's family needs.

qa.q: How might Farida see Nazia's long evenings at the library?
qa.a: Probably as a sign of real determination, which is why she offers time, a routine and her own help.

grounding: A rural teenager studies for a big goal without money for coaching, and a local mentor helps her fit a plan around family needs.

passage:
Tuesday night
Power cut again. Studying by the lantern. Ammi says it'll ruin my eyes. Did 20 physics questions anyway.
I want to be an engineer. Bridges. Everyone in our village laughs a little when I say it. Abbu says, "First help with the harvest, then dream." He's not wrong. We need hands this month.
Today Divyansh Bhaiya came from the town. He cleared the JEE three years ago and now he teaches free on Sundays at the panchayat hall. He looked at my notebook and said, "Your concepts are good, Imran. You're missing practice papers." He's bringing me old ones.
He also said, "Coaching in the city costs a lot. But there are free online lectures and scholarships. We'll find a way."
I'm tired from the fields. But I did 20 questions. Tomorrow 25.
Imran

qa.q: How many physics questions did Imran do?
qa.a: Imran did 20 physics questions.

qa.q: How does Imran feel about his dream?
qa.a: Imran feels determined but tired, pulled between the harvest and his wish to become an engineer.

qa.q: How is Divyansh Bhaiya's help important?
qa.a: As a local mentor who cleared the exam, he spots Imran's gap in practice, brings old papers and points to free lectures and scholarships.

qa.q: How does Abbu seem to see Imran's dream?
qa.a: Abbu doesn't reject it, but he sees the family's immediate need for help with the harvest as coming first.

grounding: A village teenager studies by lamplight dreaming of engineering, slowed by family need and coaching gaps, and helped by a local mentor.

passage:
Every evening after the buffaloes were fed, Hemant, sixteen, climbed onto the flat roof of their house with his books and a solar lamp. Below, the village went dark early; above, the stars came out. He wanted to be an IAS officer.
His father needed him on the farm, especially now that the loan for the pump was due. Hemant didn't argue. He fed the animals at five a.m., went to school, came back, worked, then studied until his eyes watered.
One day, Shankar Guruji, the retired schoolteacher, saw him reading on the roof. He climbed up, puffing. "Hemant, you're studying the wrong books for that exam."
He came back the next day with a bag of old newspapers, maps and his own notes. "Two evenings a week, my veranda. Bring questions."
Hemant's father saw the bag. He said nothing, but that night he told Hemant to sleep an hour later and skip the morning milking.

qa.q: Where did Hemant study every evening?
qa.a: He studied on the flat roof of their house with his books and a solar lamp.

qa.q: What was Hemant's father feeling when he told Hemant to skip the morning milking?
qa.a: His father probably felt proud and moved, seeing a respected teacher invest in his son, and wanted to give him a little more rest to study.

qa.q: How did Shankar Guruji help Hemant's dream?
qa.a: He corrected Hemant's books, gave him newspapers, maps and notes, and offered regular sessions, filling the coaching gap as a local mentor.

qa.q: What is it like for Hemant to balance farm work and study?
qa.a: It is exhausting; he works from five a.m. and studies until his eyes water, but he stays determined.

grounding: A village teenager dreams of the civil services, slowed by farm work and family need, and a local mentor helps him move forward.

passage: In a village outside Hue, Mei did her physics problems by a battery lamp after the pigs were fed. She wanted to build bridges, real ones, in the city. The nearest extra classes were in town, an hour away by motorbike, and cost more than her family could spare. When her father hurt his back in the paddy, Mei missed two weeks of school to plant seedlings. She cried once, into the rice, then went back to her equations at night. At the Tet holidays, Mina came home. Mina had grown up two houses away and now worked for a road company in Da Nang. She sat with Mei on the step, looked through the notebook, and said, "Your working is neat. I'll send you my old textbooks, and we'll talk every Sunday on the phone."

qa.q: What did Mei do her physics problems by?
qa.a: She did them by a battery lamp after the pigs were fed.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling when she missed school to plant seedlings?
qa.a: Mei felt sad and frustrated, crying once into the rice, but stayed determined enough to return to the equations at night.

qa.q: Why does Mina's offer matter so much?
qa.a: Mina offers what the village lacks, old textbooks and weekly guidance, which helps fill the gap left by the costly classes in town.

qa.q: What might Mina see when looking through Mei's notebook?
qa.a: Mina probably sees real promise, and perhaps her own younger self, in the neat working, which is why she offers books and Sunday calls.

grounding: It illustrates a rural teenager studying by lamp for a city engineering dream, slowed by cost and family need, and helped by a local mentor.
